headline: New Orleans sets its taste on Magazine Street and moves its volume in the suburbs
summary: Basketball is a small business here next to football and Mardi Gras. The Saints and local city-pride brands own the Gulf South gear wallet, and the Pelicans sit below them. Taste lives in a few uptown and Bywater shops and at pop-ups. Volume lives in Metairie, Gretna and Kenner, and online. The job is to earn city-pride credibility, not to add square footage.

insights.title: City pride outsells the Pelicans
insights.detail: Locals wear fleur-de-lis, 'Who Dat' and NOLA-pride tees from brands like Dirty Coast and Fleurty Girl every day. Pelicans gear fights for the same shirt-drawer slot, and fans often wear city-first, not team-first.
insights.implication: Put New Orleans iconography first and the team mark second on Pelicans and City Edition product. It should pass as city pride, not team merch.

insights.title: Taste on Magazine Street, volume in Jefferson Parish
insights.detail: Uptown Magazine Street holds the independent boutiques and vintage. The Lakeside, Riverwalk and West Bank (Oakwood) malls hold the athletic chains and department stores where families buy sneakers and jerseys.
insights.implication: Seed limited drops and collabs in tastemaker doors and local pop-ups. Then send mainstream colorways to Foot Locker, Dick's and Dillard's in the suburbs.

insights.title: Sneaker culture is community-run
insights.detail: New Orleans has fewer destination sneaker boutiques than Atlanta or Houston. The culture runs through school and AAU hoops, park courts, resale meetups and Black-owned apparel brands. Much of it sells through social media and pop-ups.
insights.implication: Fund local creators and pop-up hosts instead of a single flagship. Treat the Instagram-driven local sellers as the retail scene.

insights.title: The arena store is a game-night door
insights.detail: The Pelicans Team Store at Smoothie King Center and the arena's pop-up kiosks catch event-night buyers. The season-ticket base is modest after two sub-30-win seasons and a new coach, Jamahl Mosley. Fanatics and the team's online store carry the rest of the team-gear volume.
insights.implication: Use the arena store for City Edition launches, Zion and Trey Murphy III player-tee drops and Cup-night giveaways. Keep deep inventory online.

insights.title: Tourists skew the Quarter and Canal Street
insights.detail: Canal Place, Riverwalk and the Quarter's souvenir shops see huge traffic. It is visitor spend on Saints, Mardi Gras and generic NOLA gear, not local basketball demand.
insights.implication: Treat tourist districts as places for brand visibility and Mardi Gras-season merchandising. Don't read them as a gauge of local Pelicans demand.

insights.title: Black Masking Indian imagery is off limits without a deal
insights.detail: Suits, feathers and beadwork belong to specific Black neighborhood tribes and the social aid and pleasure clubs. The community guards how they are used, and commercial lifting without credit has drawn criticism.
insights.implication: Work only through paid collaboration with named artists and clubs. Keep product abstracted from ceremonial imagery.

places.name: Smoothie King Center
places.why: Home of the Pelicans and the Pelicans Team Store, the top team-branded door for game-night buyers.

places.name: Magazine Street
places.why: Six miles of independent boutiques, vintage and local-brand shops that set taste for style-conscious shoppers.

places.name: Lakeside Shopping Center
places.why: The suburban mall where Jefferson Parish families buy sneakers and team gear at the chains and Dillard's.

places.name: Riverwalk Outlets
places.why: Riverfront outlet mall, heavy with tourists, near the convention center and arena corridor.

places.name: Oakwood Center
places.why: The main West Bank mall, serving a large Black and working-class base of sneaker buyers.

places.name: St. Claude Avenue corridor
places.why: An art-and-music corridor where pop-ups, markets and local makers turn up.

places.name: Frenchmen Art Market
places.why: An evening market of local makers and artists, a natural spot for small collabs and artist pop-ups.

places.name: Dillard University
places.why: One of the city's HBCU anchors alongside Xavier, and a source of young Black shoppers and homecoming-season demand.

people.name: Zion Williamson
people.why: The franchise's biggest jersey and sneaker draw. His availability moves team-gear sales more than anything else.

people.name: Trey Murphy III
people.why: A breakout scorer averaging 21.5 ppg and the most credible second face for team product.

people.name: Derik Queen
people.why: A young piece of the post-Zion core, for second-year-player and youth product.

people.name: Jeremiah Fears
people.why: A young guard who gives sneakers and apparel a youth storyline.

people.name: Big Freedia
people.why: Queen of Bounce and its best-known face, a high-credibility pop-up collaborator if approached and paid properly.

people.name: Dirty Coast
people.why: A long-running New Orleans pride brand with Magazine Street retail, and an obvious partner for city-first graphics.

people.name: Fleurty Girl
people.why: A homegrown NOLA tee and gift brand with a devoted local following and several local doors.

moments.name: Pelicans home opener and City Edition launch
moments.why: The first window to sell new uniforms and player tees at the arena and in local doors.

moments.name: NBA Cup West Group B nights
moments.why: The Pelicans open Cup play at the Clippers on Oct 30. Home Cup nights are giveaway and merchandise moments.

moments.name: Holiday gifting
moments.why: Peak seasonal volume for jerseys, hoodies and sneakers, at malls and online.

moments.name: Carnival season and Mardi Gras
moments.why: The peak season for tourist and local merch, and the city's biggest cultural moment. Purple, green and gold fill every shop.

moments.name: New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Festival
moments.why: A huge season for pop-ups and collabs, with a local and visitor crowd and a traditional venue for Black-owned makers.

moments.name: Essence Festival of Culture
moments.why: A major Black cultural and consumer event around the Superdome and Smoothie King Center, and a prime window for brand and retail launches.

moments.name: Saints season
moments.why: Competes directly for fan spend and storefront space through the fall.

designCues.cue: Mardi Gras purple, green and gold used as accent rather than full palette
designCues.source: Carnival's official colors, everywhere on city merchandise
designCues.use: Use as trim and lining accents on Pelicans product. It nods to the city without looking like novelty gear.

designCues.source: Mardi Gras color scheme and Pelicans' own gold
designCues.use: Pair with Pelicans navy for a city-first colorway.
The base for Association and Icon products, with the city cue as accent.

designCues.cue: Fleur-de-lis in a restrained, non-Saints execution
designCues.source: City emblem in common local use
designCues.use: Emboss it or print it tonal, so it reads as city, not Saints.

designCues.source: French Quarter and Garden District architecture
designCues.use: A fine-line tonal repeat on warm-ups or linings.

designCues.source: Local corner stores, po-boy shops and second-line banners
designCues.use: Inspiration for capsule wordmarks named for neighborhoods.

designCues.cue: Brass band and second-line parade energy
designCues.source: Tremé and Seventh Ward social aid and pleasure club tradition
designCues.use: Tell the story through collaboration and credit, not sacred or ceremonial imagery.

productHooks: A neighborhood-name capsule (Seventh Ward, Tremé, Central City, West Bank) made with local graphic artists. Sell it first through Magazine Street and St. Claude partners and pop-ups.
Zion and Trey Murphy III player tees and hoodies, timed to the home opener and Cup nights at the arena store.
A Mardi Gras-season city-pride drop in tonal fleur-de-lis and Carnival accents, sold through local brands like Dirty Coast and Fleurty Girl.
A youth pack for Jefferson Parish and West Bank school and AAU hoops, sold through Dick's and the mall chains.
An Essence Festival weekend capsule with Black New Orleans designers and artists, paid and credited.
watchouts: Don't use Mardi Gras Indian suit, feather or beadwork imagery without a paid collaboration with named tribe members or artists.
Fleur-de-lis and 'Who Dat' overlap with Saints and New Orleans Saints licensing. Confirm any Saints-adjacent marks before use.
Tourist-district sales are not local Pelicans demand. Don't plan around them.
Pelicans fandom is thinner after two sub-30-win seasons. Don't overstock team-branded volume.

districts.name: Magazine Street (Uptown to Garden District)
districts.profile: A long corridor of independent boutiques, vintage, local brands and cafes.
districts.shopper: Style-conscious locals, Tulane students, young professionals and visitors.

districts.name: Bywater / Marigny / St. Claude Avenue
districts.profile: An arts-and-music corridor with markets, galleries and pop-up-friendly spaces.

districts.name: Lakeside Shopping Center (Metairie)
districts.profile: A suburban enclosed mall anchored by Dillard's, with athletic and sneaker chains.
districts.shopper: Jefferson Parish families, teens and mainstream sneaker buyers.

districts.name: Oakwood Center (Gretna)
districts.profile: A West Bank mall anchored by a department store and chains.
districts.shopper: West Bank families and working-class shoppers, with a strong Black consumer base.

districts.name: Riverwalk Outlets and Canal Place
districts.profile: A riverfront outlet mall and an upscale downtown mall near the convention center and Quarter.
districts.shopper: Tourists, convention visitors and some locals.

districts.name: Smoothie King Center and CBD
districts.profile: The arena district, next to the Superdome.

doors.name: Pelicans Team Store at Smoothie King Center

doors.name: Dirty Coast
doors.why: A beloved local pride brand and the clearest city-first collab partner.

doors.name: Fleurty Girl

doors.name: Foot Locker (Lakeside and other Jefferson Parish doors)

doors.name: Dick's Sporting Goods (Metairie area)

doors.name: Dillard's (Lakeside and Oakwood)
